questions.stem: Mrs Halloran, 52, comes to your suburban GP clinic. She woke two days ago with hearing loss in her left ear. Otoscopy is normal in both ears. You do Weber and Rinne tests with a 512 Hz tuning fork. Which pair of findings points to a left sensorineural loss?
options: Weber lateralises to the left; Rinne negative on the left
Weber lateralises to the right; Rinne positive on both sides
Weber lateralises to the left; Rinne positive on both sides
Weber is central; Rinne negative on the left
questions.why: In sensorineural loss the Weber is heard in the better (right) ear, and the Rinne stays positive on both sides because the middle ear still conducts air better than bone. Tuning forks only screen, so confirm with an audiogram.
notes: This is the pattern for a left conductive loss, such as wax or an effusion: the sound goes to the affected ear and bone conduction beats air conduction.
A Weber that goes to the left with a positive Rinne on both sides does not fit either pattern; a left sensorineural loss sends the Weber away from the left ear.
A central Weber means the two ears are symmetrical, and a negative left Rinne would mean a conductive loss, so this fits neither picture.

questions.stem: Mrs Halloran, 52 and 72 kg, has a new left sensorineural loss of 40 to 70 dB on today's audiogram, which started two days ago. She has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.4%) and an eGFR of 87. You have contacted ENT and requested an MRI of the internal auditory canals. What is the most appropriate treatment to start in general practice today?
options: Hold steroids until MRI excludes a vestibular schwannoma, then start prednisolone
Oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for 5 days, a lower dose because of her diabetes
Oral valaciclovir with prednisolone to cover a viral cochleitis after her cold
Oral prednisolone about 1 mg/kg (capped near 60 to 70 mg) each morning, then taper
questions.why: Start high-dose oral prednisolone (about 1 mg/kg, capped at the local maximum) the same day, without waiting for the MRI, because earlier treatment gives a better chance of recovery. Diabetes is a reason to plan glucose monitoring, not to lower the dose.
notes: The MRI must not delay steroids. Treatment is time-critical, and the MRI is still needed later whatever the response.
Lowering the dose because of diabetes undertreats a time-critical condition. The answer is to monitor and manage her glucose, not to reduce the steroid.
Antivirals have not been shown to help in sudden sensorineural hearing loss and are not recommended, even after a viral illness.

questions.stem: Mrs Halloran, 52, has type 2 diabetes on metformin. She will start prednisolone 60 mg at 8 am with breakfast for sudden sensorineural hearing loss. Her BGL this morning is 8.2 mmol/L. Which mechanism best explains the glucose pattern you warn her to expect?
options: Hepatic gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, peaking in the afternoon and evening
Glucagon surge overnight, causing the highest readings fasting on waking
Direct beta-cell toxicity, causing sustained absolute insulin deficiency
Reduced metformin absorption, raising glucose evenly across the whole day
questions.why: Glucocorticoids increase hepatic gluconeogenesis and cause peripheral insulin resistance. A morning dose of prednisolone raises glucose mainly in the afternoon and evening, so that is when she should check her BGL, and fasting readings may stay near baseline.
notes: A single morning dose of prednisolone mostly wears off overnight, so fasting readings are usually the least affected. A peak on waking is the opposite of the usual pattern.
Steroids impair insulin action and secretion reversibly. They do not destroy beta cells or cause absolute insulin deficiency like type 1 diabetes.
Prednisolone does not meaningfully reduce metformin absorption, and the rise in glucose is not even across the day; it follows the timing of the dose.

questions.stem: Mrs Halloran, 52, has diabetes and hypertension, her mother had a stroke, and she was briefly unsteady yesterday. She now has sudden left sensorineural hearing loss. You consider an anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) stroke. Why can an AICA infarct cause sudden one-sided hearing loss?
options: The cochlea is supplied by the stylomastoid artery, a branch of AICA
AICA supplies the primary auditory cortex in the superior temporal gyrus
The labyrinthine artery, the inner ear's end-artery supply, usually arises from AICA
AICA supplies the medial geniculate body, the thalamic relay for hearing
questions.why: The labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery usually arises from AICA. It runs with cranial nerves VII and VIII in the internal acoustic meatus and is an end artery to the cochlea and vestibule, so an AICA occlusion can cause sudden one-sided deafness and vertigo.
notes: The stylomastoid artery comes from the posterior auricular or occipital artery and supplies the middle ear and facial canal, not the cochlea.
The auditory cortex is supplied by the middle cerebral artery, and because hearing is represented on both sides, a one-sided cortical lesion does not cause one-sided deafness.
The medial geniculate body is supplied by branches of the posterior cerebral artery, and a one-sided lesion above the cochlear nuclei does not cause one-sided deafness.
